tone_statements.quote: This typological sketch of Greater Awyu phonologies is mostly based on the four languages that are relatively well-documented, one of each branch and subgroup of the family: Korowai (Becking-Dawi), Kombai (Ndeiram), Digul Wambon (Dumut) and Aghu (Awyu). Greater Awyu languages have simple and cross-linguistically very common (C)V(C) syllables (Dixon 2010: 9). The Awyu subgroup and Kombai have (C)V syllables. Word stress is a pitch-accent on the last syllable (e.g. Aghu) or penultimate syllable (e.g. Wambon). In Korowai and Kombai the pitch-accent is contrastive.

audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, final (final stress)' rests on the 2016 ANU grammar, the most recent and fullest description (Glottolog lists only it and its 1957 Dutch source). We held no copy; I downloaded the open-access PDF and confirmed the deciding quotation verbatim in sec. 1.2.3 (printed p. 21, record says p. 22 — off by one, section spans 21-22). The grammar's further stress remarks (regular suffix-final stress in verbs, lexical exceptions marked with grave accent, clitic/suffix-induced shifts, N1PL realis stem-final stress) support 'dominant, not strict' final stress. Caveat inherent to the language, not the record: all data are Drabbe's 1950s impressionistic transcription ('weak accent'); no instrumental or later fieldwork exists. Optional housekeeping: register the downloaded PDF as the copy consulted and correct the locator to p. 21-22.

sources.citation: van den Heuvel 2016, Aghu (A-PL 33), full PDF from ANU repository, sec. 1.2.3 p. 22
sources.quote: Lexical stress is on the last syllable of the word. Drabbe speaks of a "weak accent." Following Drabbe, I have not indicated stress in case it is regular, and use an accent grave to indicate stress in irregular cases, as in toxopòmu 'some'.

sources.citation: van den Heuvel, Wilco. 2016. Aghu: annotated texts with grammatical introduction and vocabulary lists. Asia-Pacific Linguistics 33. Canberra: Australian National University. hdl:1885/111412 (open access).
sources.quote: "Lexical stress is on the last syllable of the word. Drabbe speaks of a 'weak accent.' Following Drabbe, I have not indicated stress in case it is regular, and use an accent grave to indicate stress in irregular cases, as in toxopòmu 'some'. Scattered over the book, Drabbe gives several examples of stress shift to the prefinal syllable caused by 'a strong connection between a word and another element.'"

tone.quote: Drabbe refers to endocentric compounds as ‘compounds of the Germanic ‘tree trunk’ type, as found in all known Papuan languages,’ noting that the modifying noun comes first and receives stress. ... The modifying noun does not always come first in an Awyu-Dumut endocentric compound noun; it may come second in Mandobo and Aghu, and then still receives stress. ... Thus kuso is the general name for marsupials, rats and mice, while kuso-baxì means ‘kangaroo’, kuso-maxikò is a ‘field mouse’, and kuso-yowò refers to a ‘rat’ in Aghu.
